questions.question: An optimization problem has feasible set $F$ and optimal value $z^*$. When does it have multiple optimal solutions?
options: When two distinct vectors in $F$ have equal objective values
When some vector outside $F$ also attains the value $z^*$
When two optimal vectors attain different objective values
When two distinct vectors in $F$ both attain the value $z^*$

questions.question: A maximization LP has two distinct optimal solutions $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ and $\boldsymbol{y}^*$, and its objective value at $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is 160. Which statement about the optimal value and the optimal solutions is correct?
options: The optimal value 160 is unique, but the optimal solution is not.
The objective value at $\boldsymbol{y}^*$ may differ from 160.
Only the first optimal solution found counts as the optimal solution.
With two optimal solutions the LP has no single optimal value.

questions.question: In the graphical solution of a two-variable maximization LP with a finite optimum, how do multiple optimal solutions show up?
options: The objective line is parallel to a boundary line of the region.
The last objective line touches the region only at a single corner.
The last objective line meets the region along a boundary segment.
The objective line can be moved forever without leaving the region.

questions.question: For a maximization LP with optimal value 20, the feasible plans $(1,2)$ and $(3,0)$ both have objective value 12. Do they show that the LP has multiple optimal solutions?
options: Yes; two distinct feasible plans with equal values are enough.
No; they tie at 12, but only ties at the optimal value 20 count.
Yes, provided both plans satisfy every constraint of the LP.
No; distinct feasible plans can never have the same objective value.

questions.question: A production LP has a whole segment of optimal plans with the same optimal profit. The manager also prefers to make as few units of product 1 as possible. How does this preference affect the solution?
options: It raises the optimal profit, since an extra wish always improves the decision.
It has no effect, since the solver's first optimal plan must be used.
It selects one plan from the optimal segment, keeping the optimal profit.
It cannot be used, since optimal plans of an LP must all be identical.

questions.question: Giapetto maximizes $2x_s+2x_t$ subject to $2x_s+x_t\le100$, $x_s+x_t\le80$, $x_s\le40$ and $x_s,x_t\ge0$, where $x_s,x_t$ are weekly soldiers and trains. The plans $(0,80)$ and $(20,60)$ both reach the optimal value 160. Is the plan $(10,70)$ optimal?
options: No; an optimal plan must be a corner of the region.
No; it uses all 80 carpentry hours, so it is infeasible.
Only if the solver happens to report it as optimal.
Yes; it satisfies every constraint and also gives 160.

questions.question: The region $x_1+2x_2\le8$, $3x_1+x_2\le9$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has corners $(0,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(2,3)$ and $(0,4)$. For which objective does maximization over this region have multiple optimal solutions?

On the region $x_1+x_2\le7$, $x_1\le5$, $x_2\le4$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, maximizing $x_1+x_2$ gives the optimal value 7 along the edge from $(3,4)$ to $(5,2)$. The objective is changed to $0.9x_1+x_2$. What is optimal now?
options: Only $(5,2)$, with value 6.5
Only $(3,4)$, with value 6.7
The whole edge from $(3,4)$ to $(5,2)$
Only $(4,3)$, the middle of that edge

questions.question: For Giapetto's constraints $2x_s+x_t\le100$, $x_s+x_t\le80$, $x_s\le40$, $x_s,x_t\ge0$ and the objective $4x_s+2x_t$, the plan $(20,60)$ is optimal with value 200. Which other plan is also optimal?

For maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_1\le4$, $x_2\le5$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, the optimal value is 6. The points $(1,5)$, $(3,3)$, $(4,2)$ and $(5,1)$ all give $x_1+x_2=6$. Which of them are optimal solutions?
options: All four, since each reaches the value 6
Only $(1,5)$ and $(4,2)$, the two end points of the edge
Only $(3,3)$, the most balanced of them

questions.question: In a two-variable maximization LP over a bounded region, the objective line is parallel to one edge of the feasible region. Does the LP therefore have multiple optimal solutions?
options: Yes; any edge parallel to the objective line is entirely optimal
Only if that edge is where the objective line last touches the region
No; a parallel edge always makes the objective unbounded instead
No; an LP over a bounded region always has a unique optimal solution

questions.question: For maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le4$, $x_1\le2$, $x_2\le2$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, one analyst finds the optimum where $x_1+x_2=4$ and $x_1=2$ meet, another where $x_1=2$ and $x_2=2$ meet. Does the LP have multiple optimal solutions?
options: No; both pairs of boundaries meet at the same point $(2,2)$.
Yes; two different pairs of active constraints give two optima.
Yes; three active constraints always mean a whole edge.
No; with three active constraints there is no optimum.

questions.question: A solver reports one optimal plan for a production LP. Which conclusion about other optimal plans is justified?
options: Other plans with the same optimal value may exist; the report does not rule them out.
The reported plan is the unique optimum, since a solver always returns all optimal plans.
Any other plan must earn less, since the solver compared it with the reported one.
Other optimal plans would have to be infeasible, as the solver already checked them.

questions.question: For maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le8$, $x_1\le5$, $x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$, the optimal plans form the edge from $(2,6)$ to $(5,3)$, with value 8. The constraint $x_2\ge4$ is added. What is optimal now?
options: Value 8 only at $(4,4)$, where the new limit binds
Value 8 on the shorter edge from $(2,6)$ to $(4,4)$
A value below 8, since an extra constraint was added
Value 8 only at $(2,6)$, the old optimum that is left

questions.question: For minimize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge4$, $x_1\le3$, $x_2\le3$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, what are the optimal value and the optimal solutions?
options: Value 4, but at the two corners $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$ only
Value 4, only at the balanced point $(2,2)$ of that line
Value 0, at the origin $(0,0)$ where both variables are zero
Value 4, on the whole line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(3,1)$

questions.question: For maximize $4x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+x_2\le11$, $x_1\le5$, $x_2\le7$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, the optimal value 22 is attained along the edge from $(2,7)$ to $(5,1)$. Among the optimal plans, the manager wants the one with the smallest $x_2$. Which plan is chosen?

A two-variable LP over a bounded feasible region has multiple optimal solutions when its objective is maximized. Must minimizing the same objective over the same region also have multiple optimal solutions?
options: Yes; parallel edges of a region always come in opposite pairs.
No; the maximum may be an edge while the minimum is one corner.
No; a minimum and a maximum can never both be attained over one region.
Yes; ties at one end of the objective force ties at the other.

questions.question: A maximization LP with objective $f$ has optimal value $z^*$ and many optimal plans. Among them, the planner wants one with the smallest value of a second quantity $g$. Which procedure achieves this?
options: Minimize $g$ over all feasible plans of the original LP, ignoring $f$
Set every variable not in $g$ to zero and solve again
Minimize $g$ over the feasible plans with $f$ equal to $z^*$
Average all optimal plans, since they share the value $z^*$

questions.question: Consider maximize $x_1-x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\le2$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$; the feasible region is unbounded. Which statement about its optimal solutions is correct?
options: There is no finite optimum, since the feasible region is unbounded in some direction.
The optimal value is 2, attained only at the corner $(2,0)$.
The objective is unbounded, since $(t,t)$ is feasible for every $t$.
The optimal value is 2, attained at every point $(2+t,t)$ with $t\ge0$.

questions.question: The region $x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_1\le4$, $x_2\le5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has corners $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(4,2)$, $(1,5)$ and $(0,5)$. For which values of $c$ does maximizing $cx_1+x_2$ over it have multiple optimal solutions?
options: For $c=0$ and for $c=1$
For $c=1$ only
For $c=0$ only
For every $c$ from 0 to 1
